pronunciation.approximation: 'NEE-shee-nah-kah-hee-meh' — the 'r' of older romanizations is absent; all vowels are short.

kin.label: Japanese
kin.form: 日子波邇夜須毘売命 (Nishinakahime-no-mikoto), a kami of rice and agriculture

pronunciation.note: Nishinakahime is Tier 2: plain Hepburn. She is a minor agricultural kami mentioned in the imperial chronicles.

domains.title: Princess of the Rice Fields
domains.subtitle: Agriculture, Fertility, and the Sun's Gift
domains.lead: Nishinakahime is a kami of rice and agriculture whose name evokes the sun, the middle of the fields, and the princess who receives and nurtures the grain. Though less famous than Amaterasu or Inari, she belongs to the deep layer of Japanese agricultural devotion that treats the rice plant itself as divine.

cards.name: Rice Goddess
cards.desc: She governs the growth and abundance of rice.

cards.name: Solar Agriculture
cards.desc: Her name links the sun with the fertility of the fields.

cards.name: Imperial Rites
cards.desc: Agricultural kami like her are honored in court and village rituals.

cards.name: Field Guardian
cards.desc: She protects the middle plots where rice grows tall.

symbols.name: Sun
symbols.meaning: The light and warmth necessary for the harvest

symbols.name: Water
symbols.meaning: The irrigation that brings rice to fullness

mythology.lead: Nishinakahime's mythology is embedded in the agricultural theology of the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki rather than in a separate narrative cycle.

myths.title: Agricultural Kami
myths.text: The imperial chronicles name numerous kami associated with rice, fields, and the processes of cultivation. Nishinakahime belongs to this layer of agricultural divinity, representing the rice field as a sacred space nurtured by sun and water.

myths.title: Harvest Rites
myths.text: Agricultural kami were honored in imperial harvest rituals and in local festivals marking planting and reaping. The rice crop was understood as a gift from the kami and a mirror of cosmic order.

myths.title: Field Protectors
myths.text: Village religion assigned protective kami to fields, boundaries, and water sources. Figures like Nishinakahime preserve the memory of a time when every stage of rice cultivation had its divine guardian.

lore.syncretism: Nishinakahime overlaps with the broader cult of rice kami, including Inari and Toyouke-ōmikami. She is not independently prominent but represents the distributed agricultural piety that underlies Japanese Shinto.
lore.culturalLegacy: Nishinakahime is not widely known outside scholarly contexts, but her type — the agricultural kami of the rice field — remains central to Shinto's relationship with the land and the harvest.
lore.extendedMeditation: Nishinakahime is the princess of the middle field, the place where sun and water and human labor meet. She reminds us that every bowl of rice is the product of a vast collaboration between heaven, earth, and work.

sources.name: Kojiki and Nihon Shoki (agricultural kami references)

lore.archaeology: Nishinakahime has no independent archaeological record. Her significance is preserved in the textual lists of agricultural kami and in the ritual landscape of rice cultivation.
